chapter: Split, hospital and decline of tap
title: What a Jazz Monitor was
summary: Green explains the Jazz Monitor as a stand-in understudy and lists acts Harold Kroma covered, saying Sammy Davis Jr. learned from him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Well, that's just a form of -- a type of performer that could -- he could intervene -- intravene -- intervene for some other performer if some other performer is not there at show time. The Jazz Monitor could actually go out there and, you know -- like the mirror of something else. You know, he can actually -- he can do the part, like an under study or stand in, you know.
And that's what Harold Kroma was?
Yes, that's why they call him the Jazz
He would do that for other acts, too?
Yeah, he -- that's how Sammy Davis, Jr., was educating himself, by the Jazz Monitor, Harold Kroma.
What other acts did Harold Kroma -- was he the Jazz Monitor for?

Oh, several of them. (unintelligible) Them guys -- Who were they? -- they called themselves Red and Struggy, you see. That was here recently, but at the time he's talking about there weren't any Stump and Stumpy yet, see. Yes, some trio, I think he had -- yes, the Habits, the Three Habits, you know. He did that. Shorty Matthews' act, you know. Yeah, I think he did some runner-ups for the Berry Brothers, too, a few times, you know. There was some other act -- I'm trying to be very accurate about this act because they was so colorful -- they dressed like -- you could see them coming from a mile away, they was so bright, you know. What was that act's title?
